PayStream replaces the monolithic PayGate v3 payment gateway, targeting 50,000 TPS sustained (burst to 80,000) with sub-second domestic payment latency (p99 < 800ms).
The system uses a hybrid communication model: synchronous gRPC for the merchant-facing authorisation path and asynchronous Kafka events for downstream processing (settlement, ledger, notifications).
A fully synchronous architecture was rejected due to fragile dependency chains at scale; a fully asynchronous merchant API was rejected because merchants expect synchronous authorisation responses.

The payment lifecycle uses an orchestration-based saga pattern via the Payment Orchestrator, chosen over choreography due to the complex branching in payment flows (partial captures, split refunds, chargebacks).
Cardholder data is isolated in a dedicated Card Vault service running in a separate PCI-scoped network segment, reducing PCI DSS audit scope to just the Vault and API Gateway TLS termination.
Each service owns its own database (database-per-service pattern); the Ledger uses PostgreSQL with serialisable isolation for double-entry accounting integrity.
Event sourcing was considered but rejected for the Ledger in favour of traditional double-entry accounting models, which are better understood by the team.
Downstream services are eventually consistent with authorisation decisions, with up to 5 seconds of lag accepted as a trade-off.
The migration from PayGate v3 follows a strangler-fig pattern over 12 months in 4 phases, starting with 5% domestic traffic routing to PayStream.
Rollback to PayGate v3 is possible within 5 minutes at each migration phase via API Gateway feature flags, with data consistency maintained through a shared Kafka event log.
The Card Vault is a critical single-primary dependency; a primary failure blocks new card authorisations. Mitigation is automatic failover with a warm standby (RTO: 30 seconds).
The FX Service caches exchange rates with a 60-second TTL, creating a staleness risk during high-volatility periods. Mitigation is reducing TTL to 15 seconds when rate-of-change monitoring triggers.
The team has limited Kafka operational experience, identified as a medium-likelihood, high-impact risk. Mitigation is engaging a specialist consultant for 6 months.
Migrating 7 years of PayGate v3 transaction history to the new Ledger is risky due to data format differences. Mitigation is running parallel ledgers for 3 months with daily reconciliation.
The authorisation latency budget is 750ms at p99, with the acquiring bank round-trip (via Card Vault) consuming the largest share at 500ms.
Kafka topics are partitioned by merchant_id to preserve per-merchant ordering, starting at 120 partitions with a scale-out plan to 240.
Security measures include mTLS between all services, TLS 1.3 externally, AES-256 at rest, HSM-managed keys for the Card Vault, and 24-hour certificate rotation.
The technology stack spans Go (Orchestrator, Card Vault, FX), Python (Fraud Engine ML), and Java (Ledger), running on Kubernetes (EKS) with Terraform and ArgoCD.
Cryptocurrency support and physical point-of-sale integration are explicitly out of scope for the initial release.
The Reconciliation Service performs daily batch matching of internal ledger entries against bank statements, with Kafka-based exception handling.
